CHAPTER 15: HUMAN RIGHTS IN THE WIDER WORLD

LEARNING OUTCOME 6.1: RIGHTS IN THE WIDER WORLD
- Summarise research evidence on how far these UNCRC rights are implemented around the world:
- Article 6: the right to survival and development.
- Article 14: the right to freedom of thought, conscience and to have and manifest religion or beliefs.
- Article 19: the right to protection from physical or mental violence, injury, neglect or abuse.
- Article 31: the right to rest, leisure, play and recreation.
- Summarise the main rights in the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and how people can get these rights enforced.
- Critically evaluate qualitative and quantitative research on human rights.
- (Articles 28 and 29 on education were covered in Chapter 11.)

15.1 UNCRC ARTICLE 6: THE RIGHT TO SURVIVAL AND DEVELOPMENT
- Article 6.1: States recognise that every child has the inherent right to life.
- Article 6.2: States shall ensure to the maximum extent possible the survival and development of the child.
- Children should grow up in conditions that do not harm their physical and mental wellbeing.
- The right to life includes good health, development, nutritious food and clean drinking water.
- Child mortality: the death of children under five; a key indicator of a country's ability to protect the right to survival and development; measured per 1,000 live births.
- UNICEF: remarkable progress since 1990. In 2021, 1 in 26 children died before age five, compared with 1 in 11 in 1990.
- But big disparities remain. Sub-Saharan Africa: under-five mortality was 73 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2021. 1 in 14 children there died before age five - 15 times higher than in high-income countries and 20 years behind the world average (which reached 1 in 14 by 2001).

CASE STUDY: THE STRUGGLE FOR SURVIVAL FOR CHILDREN IN SOUTH SUDAN
- South Sudan has arguably failed to protect children's rights under Article 6. Human Rights Watch called it an issue of grave concern needing immediate attention.
- UNICEF, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) and Human Rights Watch have criticised the government's failure to ensure children's wellbeing.
- UNICEF: the humanitarian crisis in South Sudan is a child rights crisis. South Sudan ratified the UNCRC in 2015, but its commitments are not being met.
- Rights are interrelated: without education, children lose protection from exploitation and child labour; without clean water, health care or enough food, the right to life is compromised.
- Under-five mortality: 98.7 deaths per 1,000 live births - one of the highest in the world; about 1 in 10 children die before their fifth birthday.
- About 1.4 million children under five face severe and moderate malnutrition.
- 51% of children use water from limited or unimproved sources; most live where open defecation is practised.
- Children face malaria, pneumonia and vaccine-preventable disease - far from the 'highest attainable standard of health'.
- Causes: years of prolonged conflict, vulnerabilities, limited essential services and weak governance.
- Human Development Index (HDI): a composite measure to compare countries' development and wellbeing, using health, education and standard of living. South Sudan ranked 185 out of 189 in 2021.

15.2 UNCRC ARTICLE 14: FREEDOM OF THOUGHT, CONSCIENCE AND RELIGION
- Children, as rights holders, have the right to their own thoughts and ideas, to form and freely express opinions, including religious or non-religious beliefs and political views.
- Children, like adults, can explore different ideas, religions and philosophies; it respects individuality.
- This right comes with responsibilities: children should respect others' rights and beliefs and be tolerant.
- Article 14.1: States respect the child's right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
- Article 14.2: States respect the rights and duties of parents/guardians to give direction to the child in line with the child's evolving capacities.
- Article 14.3: Freedom to manifest religion or beliefs can only be limited by law where necessary to protect public safety, order, health, morals, or others' fundamental rights.
- In countries like Ireland, children can express opinions and beliefs without fear and have education encouraging critical thinking.
- In countries with oppressive non-democratic regimes or religious extremism, children may face censorship, surveillance or persecution.
- Irish link (Ch 14): Does the high number of religious-ethos schools limit Article 14 in Ireland? Is the right to opt out of religious instruction an example of Article 14 being realised?

CASE STUDY: THE RIGHTS OF GIRLS IN AFGHANISTAN
- Under Taliban rule, girls' rights are severely restricted. The Taliban's strict interpretation of Islamic law harms girls' freedom of thought, conscience and religion, restricting education, freedom of movement and free expression.
- UNESCO 2023: 2.5 million (80%) of school-aged Afghan girls and young women out of school; 1.2 million denied access to secondary schools and universities by the de facto authorities.
- De facto authorities: individuals or groups that control a territory or government without legal or formal recognition.
- These decisions threaten to wipe out 20 years of development gains.
- 2001 to 2021: enrolment at all levels rose tenfold, from about 1 million to about 10 million, with international support including UNESCO.
- Girls in primary school rose from almost zero to 2.5 million.
- Women in higher education rose almost 20 times, from 5,000 to over 100,000.
- Female literacy almost doubled, from 17% in 2001 to nearly 30%.
- Taliban officials say the secondary ban is temporary, giving excuses from lack of funds to remodelling the syllabus on Islamic lines.
- UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence Against Children, 24 March 2022: 'Today is a dark day for millions of girls in Afghanistan'; girls in sixth grade and above had education suspended; at least 1 million girls deprived; 'The deprivation of education is, in itself, a form of violence against girls'; the country is losing its youth, talent and energy.
- UN reminder to the Taliban (2022): they remain bound by international human rights law and humanitarian law, which promote education for all and prohibit attacks on schools and hospitals; they must protect children and respect the UNCRC, which defines a child as anyone under 18.
- Girls and women protested outside the Ministry of Education against the school closures.

15.3 UNCRC ARTICLE 19: PROTECTION FROM VIOLENCE, INJURY, NEGLECT OR ABUSE
- All children as rights holders have a fundamental right to live free from harm and grow up in a safe, nurturing environment.
- Duty bearers: governments, parents, society, teachers and caregivers must listen and respond to children's concerns.
- Children should be able to speak up about violence or abuse and be taken seriously.
- Article 19.1: States shall take all appropriate legislative, administrative, social and educational measures to protect the child from all forms of physical or mental violence, injury, abuse, neglect, maltreatment or exploitation, including sexual abuse, while in anyone's care.
- Article 19.2: Measures include social programmes to support children and carers, prevention, identification, reporting, referral, investigation, treatment, follow-up and judicial involvement.
- Irish links: Direct Provision (Ch 7) and child homelessness (Ch 6).

CASE STUDY: CHILDREN IN THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO (DRC)
- Long-standing conflict and instability between government and rebel groups has devastated children's lives.
- UNICEF: despite vast natural resources, the DRC is one of the poorest countries in the world. Extreme poverty, economic crisis, conflict, food insecurity and epidemics like Ebola harm women and children most.
- Third largest population in Africa: about 98 million people, almost 54% children.
- Progress made on infant mortality and education, but most children are still deprived of their rights; violence against children is widespread in families, schools and communities.
- UNICEF 2022 figures:
- Nearly 26.4 million people, including 15.4 million children, need urgent humanitarian help.
- 7 out of 100 children die before age five.
- More than 7 million children aged 5 to 17 are out of school.
- 33 million rural people lack safe drinking water.
- 59.9% of children under five are not registered at birth.
- 9 million children suffer chronic malnutrition or stunting.
- Nearly 1 in 3 women affected by child marriage, often linked to early pregnancy.
- 8 out of 10 children under 14 are regularly subjected to physical punishment.
- 15% of children aged 5 to 17 are in child labour.
- About 10,000 children still associated with armed groups and forced labour.
- Mining: the DRC has some of the world's richest mineral deposits - gold, tin and cobalt. Cobalt is essential for batteries in smartphones, laptops and electric cars, making billions for corporations such as Apple and Samsung. Some workers earn as little as nine cents a day in dangerous conditions.
- UNICEF (2014): about 40,000 boys and girls worked in mines across southern DRC, many in cobalt mining.
- Amnesty International (2014): children worked up to 12 hours a day carrying heavy loads for one to two dollars a day; even schoolchildren worked 10-12 hours at weekends and holidays.
- Example: Patrice, 15, began working in a gold mine at age eight.
- There is a clear link between child cobalt mining and demand from consumers and corporations, mainly in the Western world (more in Ch 22 on globalisation).
- 2 June 2023: 18 children, supported by UNICEF, World Vision and Save the Children, met the President of the DRC Senate to set up a Children's Parliament and make recommendations:
- Violence against children is at epidemic levels; failing to prevent it is akin to condoning it.
- Passing laws is not enough; success should be measured by the number of convictions, not the number of laws.
- Raise awareness of internet dangers and online reporting mechanisms.
- As a 'pathfinding country' to end violence against children, ban all violence against children in homes, schools, communities and public spaces.
- Align national law with the UNCRC.

15.4 UNCRC ARTICLE 31: THE RIGHT TO REST, LEISURE, PLAY AND RECREATION
- Known as 'the forgotten article of the Convention'. Few national reports to the UN Committee include it, and those that do focus mostly on physical activity.
- Recognises every child's right to rest, leisure, play, recreation and free and full participation in cultural and artistic life.
- Article 31.1: right to rest, leisure, play and recreation appropriate to age, and to take part in cultural life and the arts.
- Article 31.2: States shall promote full participation in cultural and artistic life and encourage equal opportunities for cultural, artistic, recreational and leisure activity.
- The UN Committee is concerned at poor recognition by governments. Threats: rising urban populations, poverty, violence, commercialisation of play, child labour and increasing educational demands.
- Investment tends to go to structured activities, but time and space for spontaneous play, recreation and creativity are equally important, as are supportive social attitudes.
- Play is central to how a child takes part in the world. Article 31 underpins healthy development, wellbeing, quality of life, socio-cultural participation, resilience and creativity.
- The right to play is interdependent with the rights to health and education (links to indivisibility).

BARRIERS TO REALISING ARTICLE 31
- Lack of recognition of the importance of play.
- Lack of political commitment.
- The political environment is linked to the economic environment, as funding follows legislation and policy.
- Unsafe and hazardous environments.
- Resistance to children's use of public spaces.
- Lack of access to nature.
- Pressure for educational achievement.
- Lack of investment in cultural and artistic opportunities.
- Poverty and deprivation.
- Children in poverty: homelessness or overcrowded homes leave little room for play; lack of facilities, cost of participation, dangerous neighbourhoods, need to work and a sense of powerlessness exclude the poorest children.
- Children with disabilities: exclusion from school or activities; negative attitudes and stereotypes; physically inaccessible environments. A scoping review found few national guidelines for inclusive playground design, leading to playgrounds not designed for varied abilities.
- Social attitudes: debates over 'acceptable play'; families feel unwelcome, stigmatised and ostracised. In one study, parents of children with autism felt judged in public playgrounds and tried to make sure their child played 'appropriately'.
- Example image: Yemeni children studying inside a war-destroyed school in Taiz city, 2020.

IRELAND'S NATIONAL PLAY POLICY
- Ireland was one of the first European countries to produce a detailed national play policy: 'Ready, Steady, Play! A National Play Policy' (March 2004), to honour UNCRC commitments (ratified 1992).
- Shows the government as duty bearer recognising play, and committing to equitable, inclusive play, especially for marginalised, disadvantaged and disabled children. It is currently being reviewed.
- A 2017 online survey of 16 European countries found play policies only in Ireland and the UK (Northern Ireland, Wales, Scotland and England).

CASE STUDY: THE PLAY SUFFICIENCY DUTY, WALES
- Wales became the first country in the world to legislate for children's play, with a Play Sufficiency Duty informed by the UNCRC.
- In 2010 the Welsh government placed a statutory duty on every local authority to assess and secure sufficient play opportunities.
- Part of the Welsh anti-poverty agenda: children can have a poverty of experience, opportunity and aspiration, which can affect children from all backgrounds.
- The second part of the Duty included better access to play for children with disabilities.
- Supports: Statutory Guidance and a 'Play Sufficiency Assessment Toolkit' for local authorities.
- Ministerial Review of Play 2019: a 59% increase in designated play areas since the legislation began in 2011; play benefits children, families and neighbourhoods.
- Wales has taken a global lead on Article 31 through policy, legislation and funding. Play is now integrated into schools and early years settings, helping physical, social and emotional development and wellbeing.

15.5 THE COUNCIL OF EUROPE AND THE ECHR
- The Council of Europe is Europe's leading human rights organisation, headquartered in Strasbourg, France.
- It promotes freedom of expression and media, freedom of assembly, equality and protection of minorities. Campaigns: child protection, online hate speech, rights of the Roma (Europe's largest minority).
- Helps states fight corruption and terrorism and carry out judicial reform. The Venice Commission, a group of constitutional experts, gives legal advice worldwide.
- Conventions include the ECHR, the Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence, and the Convention on Cybercrime. It monitors progress through independent expert bodies.
- 46 member states in 2023. Ireland joined on 5 May 1949 as a founding member.
- Russia was expelled after its invasion of Ukraine (Committee of Ministers decision, 16 March 2022).
- Debate: protecting members' sovereignty vs keeping dialogue open in a crisis.
- Convention: a legal agreement between two or more states; ratifying commits a state to its values and instructions.

KEY ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE COUNCIL OF EUROPE
- Abolition of the death penalty is a precondition of joining; no executions in member states since 1997.
- Strengthening human rights: every member agrees to independent monitoring of human rights and democracy.
- Non-discrimination: the ECHR prohibits all discrimination by public authorities on any grounds; activities to protect minorities including the Roma.
- Freedom of expression: no true democracy without free, pluralist media; European Court case-law strongly protects the press, especially confidential journalist sources.
- Gender equality: the Convention on Violence against Women and Domestic Violence is based on the idea that such violence cannot end without greater equality between women and men.
- Children's rights: the Convention for the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse is the first instrument criminalising sexual abuse of children, including at home; in force from 1 July 2010.

THE EUROPEAN CONVENTION ON HUMAN RIGHTS (ECHR)
- An international treaty adopted in 1950, in force in 1953; the first Council of Europe convention on human rights. States must ratify it to join the Council.
- International treaty: an agreement between states designed to have legal effects in their relations.
- The European Court of Human Rights is the judicial body that guarantees the Convention's rights for everyone under its jurisdiction.
- November 2022: Irish woman Siofra O'Leary became President of the European Court of Human Rights - the first female President.
- Amended over time; protocols add new rights. Its case-law means it is a 'living instrument'.
- Living instrument: the ECHR evolves over time to address changes in society, keeping protection relevant and effective.
- The ECHR protects the right to: life, freedom and security; respect for private and family life; freedom of expression; freedom of thought, conscience and religion; vote in and stand for election; a fair trial in civil and criminal matters; property and peaceful enjoyment of possessions. (The chapter also lists consolidating democratic stability through reform.)
- The ECHR prohibits: torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment; slavery and forced labour; arbitrary and unlawful detention; discrimination in enjoying Convention rights; deporting a state's own nationals or denying them entry; the death penalty; collective deportation of foreigners.

THE RIGHT OF INDIVIDUAL PETITION
- Individuals can bring complaints directly to the European Court of Human Rights about violations by a state that has ratified the Convention.
- They must first go through all the legal systems in their own country - the principle of subsidiarity.
- Crucial for access to justice and upholding human rights across Europe.

CASE STUDY: DAVID NORRIS V IRELAND (1988)
- Irish law then made male homosexual relations a criminal offence.
- David Norris, senator, gay rights activist and member of the Campaign for Homosexual Law Reform, challenged these laws.
- He argued they violated the right to privacy under Article 8 of the ECHR. He suffered anxiety attacks, deep depression and loneliness, knowing open expression of his sexuality could lead to prosecution.
- The Court found a violation of Article 8 (respect for private life). There was no 'pressing social need' to criminalise homosexual acts. Members of the public who saw it as immoral might be 'shocked, offended or disturbed', but this alone could not justify penal sanctions where consenting adults were involved.
- Former President Mary Robinson: the judgment 'was very significant because it led to a change in the criminal law'.
- 1993: after pressure from the Campaign, further challenges and public demand, the Oireachtas passed the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 1993, decriminalising sex between men.
- It helped shift attitudes and paved the way for the 2015 Marriage Equality Referendum, which made Ireland the first country to legalise same-sex marriage by popular vote (results announced at Dublin Castle, 23 May 2015).
- Other ECHR cases to research: Ireland v United Kingdom (1979-80) on torture/inhuman treatment of prisoners in Northern Ireland; A, B and C v Ireland (2010) on abortion restrictions.

COUNCIL OF EUROPE VS EUROPEAN UNION - DO NOT CONFUSE
- Council of Europe: international organisation in Strasbourg, created 1949, 46 countries; promotes democracy, human rights and the rule of law; home to the ECHR and the European Court of Human Rights.
- European Council: an institution of the EU member states; sets the EU's general political direction and priorities.
- European Court of Human Rights (Strasbourg): oversees the ECHR, final say on interpreting it; judgments binding on the states concerned.
- Court of Justice of the European Union (Luxembourg): ensures compliance with EU law.
- European Convention on Human Rights: Council of Europe treaty securing civil and political rights.
- EU Charter of Fundamental Rights: EU legal text on human rights and freedoms, adopted in 2000, largely based on the ECHR.

LINKS AND EXTRA DATA FROM EXAM QUESTIONS
- Links: Nussbaum (Ch 11), Huntington and Said (Ch 16), SDGs (Ch 23), gender roles (Ch 8), Direct Provision (Ch 7), social class (Ch 8), right to education (Ch 14).
- DRC: over 5 million conflict-related deaths recorded since 1998, with little media coverage.
- Vaccine distribution (17 June 2021): Northern America and Europe 68 doses per 100 people; Sub-Saharan Africa fewer than 2 per 100.
- Child labour: 168 million children worldwide - more than all the children in Europe.

KEY TERMS
- UNCRC Articles 6, 14, 19 and 31; child mortality; Human Development Index; Council of Europe; European Court of Human Rights; living instrument; individual petition.

rows.prompt: Study the source (UNICEF, 2022, DRC): '7 out of 100 children die before reaching the age of 5. More than 7 million children aged 5-17 are out of school. 8 out of 10 children under age 14 are regularly subjected to physical punishment. 15% of children aged 5 to 17 are engaged in child labour.' (a) What does this data reveal about the realisation of children's rights in the DRC? (b) Identify one cause of these problems. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) The data shows children's rights are widely denied in the DRC. Article 6 (survival) is not realised, as 7 in 100 children die before five. Article 19 (protection from violence) is not realised, as 8 in 10 children under 14 face regular physical punishment and 15% are in child labour. The right to education is also denied for over 7 million children. (b) One cause is long-standing conflict between the government and rebel groups, along with extreme poverty, food insecurity and epidemics like Ebola. Demand for cobalt from Western corporations also drives child labour in mines, where children earn one to two dollars a day.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 6 marks: 3 points x 2 marks, each linking a statistic to a named right. (b) 4 marks: cause identified (2 marks) and explained with evidence (2 marks).

rows.prompt: Summarise the main rights in the European Convention on Human Rights and explain one mechanism through which people can have these rights implemented. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The ECHR, adopted by the Council of Europe in 1950, protects the right to life, freedom and security; respect for private and family life; freedom of expression; freedom of thought, conscience and religion; to vote and stand for election; a fair trial; and property. It prohibits torture, slavery and forced labour, arbitrary detention, discrimination, the death penalty and collective deportation of foreigners. One mechanism is the right of individual petition: a person can bring a complaint directly to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg against a state that has ratified the Convention, once they have gone through their own country's courts (subsidiarity). David Norris used this in 1988 to win his case under Article 8.
rows.marking_scheme: Rights: 5 marks (5 correct rights or prohibitions x 1 mark). Mechanism: 5 marks (named 2 marks, explained 2 marks, example 1 mark).

rows.prompt: 'Article 31 is the forgotten article of the UNCRC.' Discuss, with reference to Ireland and one other country. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: Article 31 gives every child the right to rest, leisure, play, recreation and cultural life. It is called forgotten because few national reports to the UN Committee include it, and those that do focus mostly on physical activity. Barriers include poverty, overcrowded or homeless households, unsafe neighbourhoods, pressure for educational achievement and lack of political commitment. Children with disabilities face inaccessible playgrounds, as few national guidelines exist for inclusive design. However, some states have acted. Ireland was one of the first European countries to adopt a national play policy, 'Ready, Steady, Play!' in 2004, focusing on marginalised and disabled children; a 2017 survey of 16 countries found only Ireland and the UK had play policies. Wales went further, becoming the first country to legislate for play through the 2010 Play Sufficiency Duty, leading to a 59% increase in designated play areas by 2019. So Article 31 is neglected in most of the world but not everywhere.
rows.marking_scheme: Explanation of Article 31 and why it is 'forgotten': 3 marks. Barriers: 4 marks (2 x 2). Irish example developed: 4 marks. Other country example developed (e.g. Wales): 4 marks.

rows.prompt: 'Human rights declarations and conventions are little more than ideas on paper for children in poverty and powerlessness.' Discuss, referring to at least two thinkers and contemporary evidence. (80 marks)
rows.model_answer: Introduction: I largely agree that conventions like the UNCRC are often only words on paper for the poorest children, though they do bring some real progress. I will use Nussbaum's capabilities approach and Rawls's justice as fairness, with case studies from South Sudan, Afghanistan, the DRC and Wales. Argument 1 - survival (Article 6): South Sudan ratified the UNCRC in 2015, yet its under-five mortality is 98.7 per 1,000, 1.4 million children are malnourished, 51% use poor water sources and it ranked 185 out of 189 on the HDI in 2021. UNICEF calls it a child rights crisis. Nussbaum would say these children lack basic capabilities such as life and health, so rights on paper mean little. Argument 2 - freedom of thought (Article 14): In Afghanistan the de facto Taliban authorities left 2.5 million girls (80%) out of school by 2023, despite international law. The UN called the ban 'a form of violence against girls'. A convention cannot be enforced against a regime that ignores it. Argument 3 - protection (Article 19): In the DRC, 8 in 10 children under 14 face physical punishment, 15% are in child labour and 10,000 are with armed groups. Around 40,000 children worked in southern mines, some for one to two dollars a day, supplying cobalt to firms like Apple and Samsung. The children's delegation to the DRC Senate in 2023 said success should be measured by convictions, not laws - proving the point that paper alone is not enough. Counter-argument: Conventions do create change. Global under-five deaths fell from 1 in 11 in 1990 to 1 in 26 in 2021. Afghan enrolment rose tenfold from 2001 to 2021 with UNESCO support. Wales's Play Sufficiency Duty, informed by the UNCRC, increased play areas by 59%. In Europe the ECHR is enforceable: David Norris won at the European Court of Human Rights in 1988, leading to decriminalisation in 1993, and the Council of Europe has seen no executions since 1997. Rawls would argue rights frameworks are needed as a base of fairness. Conclusion: Where conventions have enforcement mechanisms and political will, as with the ECHR or Wales, they improve lives. For children in poverty and powerlessness under conflict or authoritarian rule, they too often remain ideas on paper, so states and the international community must act as real duty bearers.
rows.marking_scheme: SEC-style discursive marking: Clear position stated and sustained (up to 10 marks). Knowledge of UNCRC Articles 6, 14, 19, 31 and the ECHR (up to 15 marks). Use of at least two thinkers, e.g. Nussbaum, Rawls, applied to arguments (up to 15 marks). Contemporary evidence and data, e.g. UNICEF figures for South Sudan and DRC, UNESCO Afghanistan data, Wales 59%, Norris v Ireland (up to 20 marks). Counter-arguments evaluated (up to 15 marks). Structure and conclusion (up to 5 marks).
